newsitem.title: FRANCE: German car makers back drive to monetary union.
newsitem.headline: German car makers back drive to monetary union.

text.p: German's leading car makers are lining up in support of European monetary union, saying a single currency will help them be more competitive and lead to lasting economic growth.

European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), the object of increasingly intense debate in Germany, is the linchpin of the European common market and will help reduce swings in sales stemming from currency market fluctuations, the car makers say.
"I can see only advantages," BMW AG chairman Bernd Pischetsrieder told Reuters in an interview. "It will help reduce currency-related uncertainties."
The support for EMU comes at a time of severe government budget cuts throughout Europe which are slowing economic growth, hurting demand and, in the case of Germany, leading to labour unrest.
But car makers, which still have fresh memories of the problems caused by the mark's strength last year, remain die-hard Euro-optimists.
"The Euro is not an option which can either be taken or rejected," Mercedes-Benz AG chairman Helmut Werner told a group of journalists. "It is absolutely essential to our competitiveness."

The strong mark last year cost German car makers hundreds of million of marks in lost revenues as they received fewer marks from sales in other currencies and found the price of their cars climbing in markets outside Germany.

"There are too many various kinds of currencies in Europe," said Anton Hunger, spokesman for Dr.-Ing.h.c.F. Porsche AG. "It is very difficult to prepare for swings like the Italian lira takes sometimes."

The support for EMU, however, runs deeper than currency advantages, with some car makers saying it is helping to bring badly needed reforms to the German economy and will enable them to become more competitive.

Werner, for one, called on the government to redouble efforts to meet Maastricht treaty deficit criteria, slashing government subsidies and the generous system of welfare handouts that have made Germany one of the most expensive production centres in the world.
"In the long term, this is the only policy which can lead to success," Werner said.

He and others also said Japanese car makers, crippled by a strong yen in recent years, were making a comeback and that European car makers needed a broad domestic market, as the U.S. industry has, to help them withstand the coming competition.

Showing support for EMU is also clearly the "politically correct" position in Germany, where Chancellor Helmut Kohl is perhaps the greatest champion of a single currency and good relations with the government are valued highly by the industry.

EMU will offer varying degrees of benefit to German car makers. Volkswagen, for example, has units throughout Europe which help it to offset what happens to the mark alone but the Wolfsburg-based group remains behind the EMU project.
"We are fully behind EMU. It is clearly in our interests," Porsche's Hunger said.
